lesson.title: The Paperwork Format Behind Every Padlock Icon
lesson.summary: X.509 is the standardized data format used to represent digital certificates in almost every PKI deployment, defining exactly what fields a certificate must contain and how a certificate authority's signature ties them together.
lesson.body:
Public key infrastructure is a system of roles and processes: certificate authorities, registration, revocation. X.509 is the specific, standardized file format that most of that infrastructure actually uses to represent a certificate as data. Originally defined by the ITU-T standards body and now most commonly encountered in its third version, X.509v3, it specifies precisely which fields a certificate must contain and how they are laid out, so that any compliant piece of software, a browser, an email client, a server, can parse and validate a certificate issued by any compliant certificate authority, regardless of who built either piece of software.

An X.509 certificate contains a defined set of fields. There is a version number, a serial number unique to that certificate as issued by its CA, an identifier for the signature algorithm used, the issuer name identifying the CA that signed it, a validity period given as a "not before" and "not after" date, and the subject name, identifying the entity the certificate was issued to. Critically, it also contains the subject's public key information: the algorithm and the actual public key value being certified. Version 3 added support for extensions, optional additional fields such as Subject Alternative Name, which lists every domain name a certificate is valid for, Key Usage, which restricts what the key may be used for, and Basic Constraints, which states whether the certificate belongs to a CA authorized to sign other certificates or to an end entity that is not. Finally, and this is the field that makes everything else meaningful, the certificate carries the issuing CA's own digital signature, computed over all the preceding fields.

That last field is where every earlier chapter in this sequence comes together in one object. The CA computes a hash of the certificate's other fields and signs that hash with its own private key, exactly the digital signature process described several chapters back. A relying party, say a browser, verifies that signature using the CA's public key, which it trusts because that CA's own certificate chains, possibly through one or more intermediates, up to a root certificate already built into the browser's trust store. If the signature checks out, the browser accepts that the public key stated in the certificate really does belong to the subject named in it, exactly the identity-to-key binding described as the whole point of a certificate authority.

Certificates are usually stored and transmitted in one of two encodings: DER, a compact binary format, or PEM, a base64-encoded text version of DER wrapped in header and footer lines, which is the format most people actually see when they open a certificate file and find a block of text framed by "BEGIN CERTIFICATE" and "END CERTIFICATE" markers. When a browser connects to a website over TLS, the server presents its X.509 certificate as part of the handshake, and the browser runs through the whole chain: checking the signature, checking the validity dates, checking that the requested domain appears in the Subject Alternative Name field, and checking revocation status, before it will show that small padlock and let the encrypted session proceed.
